idiom_name: std::process::Command-style builder: fn arg(&mut self, ...) -> &mut Command, terminal build()/spawn()
implementation_notes: Rust builders are written by hand because every field must be present at construction and the language has neither default arguments nor overloading: a separate builder type holds one Option<T> per optional setting, each step mutates the builder and hands a borrow back, and a terminal method consumes or borrows it and reports missing values. The Rust API Guidelines prescribe this shape (C-BUILDER) and the standard library demonstrates both ownership treatments: std::process::Command takes and returns &mut self so one configured command can be spawned repeatedly, while std::thread::Builder takes and returns self so ownership of the captured closure and writer is threaded to the terminal method. Deriving the builder (typed-builder, derive_builder) is the escape hatch once the boilerplate grows.
pitfalls: Mixing the two ownership conventions does not compile: a &mut self step returns a borrow that cannot be passed to a terminal `build(self)`, so one convention must be chosen for the whole builder.
A &mut self builder cannot be stored next to the value it configures while also being returned from a function that borrows it; chained temporaries die at the end of the statement.
A builder captured across an await point or sent to another thread must be Send/Sync; sharing it through Rc or a static requires the configured state to be cloned into the product instead.

variants.name: Consuming builder (self -> Self)
variants.implementation_notes: The other documented Rust treatment: each step takes `mut self` and returns Self, and the terminal method takes self, so ownership flows through the chain and the product can take over resources (writers, closures, handles) without cloning. std::thread::Builder is the standard-library example: `Builder::new().name("worker".into()).spawn(move || work())`. This makes single-expression chains read like a pipeline, at the price of verbose conditional configuration, where each step must rebind the builder (`b = b.name(...)`); choose it when the terminal genuinely has to consume the configuration.
variants.idiom_name: std::thread::Builder style: pub fn name(mut self, n: String) -> Builder
pitfalls: In conditional configuration the builder must be rebound at every step (`b = b.name(...)`); reassigning late silently drops the earlier value and the borrow checker only reports it when the old binding is used.
A consuming step used on a borrowed builder (`(&mut b).name(...)`) does not compile - the whole chain must own its builder.
